ctx: In direct relation to the present study, the literature also shows why transformer-based modeling has become especially important. Attention mechanisms enable direct modeling of long-range dependencies, which is valuable in deepfake forensics because authenticity cues may involve relationships among distant facial regions rather than only local defects (Vaswani et al., 2017). However, fully global attention is expensive at high resolutions and long sequence lengths, which are precisely the conditions needed to preserve subtle forensic traces. Hierarchical and window-based transformers address this limitation by balancing detail preservation and contextual reasoning. ctx: Deepfake detection research sits at the intersection of synthetic media generation, digital video forensics, and deployable human-facing systems. Recent deepfake generators can produce photorealistic facial content under common online conditions such as compression, resizing, and re-encoding, which complicates authenticity judgments that historically relied on human perception and obvious editing artifacts (Dolhansky et al., 2020; Rössler et al., 2019). Consequently, contemporary detection must be framed not only as a classification task, but also as a robustness problem under distribution shift, where detectors must generalize across datasets, manipulation families, and post-processing pipelines (Jiang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020). At the same time, practical solutions increasingly take the form of web-accessible tools, which means that software quality, usability, performance efficiency, and security become part of the overall research contribution (International Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2018; ISO, 2023).

GAN-based pipelines first raised the realism of facial synthesis and manipulation, while diffusion-based models further enhanced perceptual fidelity, texture realism, and visual coherence (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020). As a result, many earlier artifact cues have become less stable across generator families and post-processing conditions. ctx: Even with stronger architectures, the literature repeatedly warns that high accuracy within a single dataset can be misleading. FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF (v2), and DeeperForensics-1.0 are important not only because they are widely used, but also because each stresses a different aspect of the detection problem. FaceForensics++ highlights the effect of compression, Celeb-DF increases realism and reduces obvious artifacts, and DeeperForensics-1.0 introduces perturbations that reflect real-world degradation. Together, these datasets show that a detector may appear strong while actually relying on shortcuts tied to collection quirks, compression settings, or preprocessing routines. Thus, cross-dataset transfer testing and perturbation-stressed evaluation are now treated as necessary safeguards against overestimating real-world robustness (Rössler et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020; Geirhos et al., 2020).

Accuracy alone is not treated as sufficient because a model may appear strong on a single dataset while still failing to generalize or while committing a problematic pattern of false positives or false negatives. Precision is important because a fake prediction should not be triggered too easily on authentic content; Recall is important because manipulated videos that evade detection directly weaken the practical value of the detector; F1-Score summarizes the Precision–Recall trade-off; and ROC-AUC evaluates discrimination behavior across thresholds rather than at a single operating point. Confusion matrices, ROC curves, FPR, and FNR are used to examine whether a model is conservative, over-sensitive, or brittle under quality degradation and dataset shift (Rössler et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020; Kingra et al., 2024).
